metadata.title: Whole Brain Susceptibility Mapping Using Harmonic Incompatibility Removal

extraction_notes.note: The theorem environment closes before its enumerated conclusions, which sit in a separate {\it enumerate} block. TP2 keeps the environment span; the two items are emitted as part-claims outside it, each with a uses edge into TP2, and the proof has proves edges to all three.

The numbered equation (2.1) is named the magnetostatic Maxwell's equation, so it was retyped as an external theorem per the named-equation rule. It is a physical law rather than a mathematical theorem.

These numbered equations are standalone optimization formulations (Frame-Int, Frame-Diff), so they were retyped as problem. The analogous formulations in prose (Tikhonov, SMV, HIRE) are problem nodes that contain their numbered equation.
The sentence both introduces the discrete Laplacian and asserts the discrete harmonic property. It is kept as one heuristic claim rather than a definition.
An align* with a \label is reported as an environment fact although it is unnumbered. It was emitted as an equation node because the rules say every fact gets its node.
The standard QSM pipeline lists four steps but describes only three in its sentence. Those three are the algorithm steps; dipole inversion is the separate problem node ProbP1 in the next paragraph.

Left out: the experimental setup (data simulation, parameter choices, stopping criterion), the figure and table content, and the discursive motivation paragraphs comparing artifact types. Only the headline experimental conclusions are kept, as numerical claims.

nodes.name: Magnetic susceptibility
nodes.statement: The magnetic susceptibility $\chi$ is an intrinsic property of the material which relates ${\mathbf M}$ and the magnetic field ${\mathbf H}=(H_1,H_2,H_3)$ through ${\mathbf M}=\chi{\mathbf H}$ \cite{J.K.Seo2014}.
nodes.genus: an intrinsic property of the material
differentia: relates ${\mathbf M}$ and the magnetic field ${\mathbf H}=(H_1,H_2,H_3)$ through ${\mathbf M}=\chi{\mathbf H}$

nodes.name: Complex GRE signal model
nodes.statement: I(\boldsymbol{x},TE)=m(\boldsymbol{x})\exp\left\{-i\left(b(\boldsymbol{x})\omega_0B_0TE+\theta_0(\boldsymbol{x})\right)\right\},
nodes.statement_short: GRE signal = magnitude times phase factor linear in total field $b$ and echo time.
nodes.label: ComplexMR

nodes.name: Phase model
nodes.statement: \theta(\boldsymbol{x})=b(\boldsymbol{x})\omega_0B_0TE+\theta_0(\boldsymbol{x}).
nodes.label: phasemodel

nodes.name: Region of interest $\Omega$
nodes.statement: Based on the observations $\theta(\boldsymbol{x})$, QSM aims at visualizing the susceptibility distribution $\chi(\boldsymbol{x})$ in the region of interests (ROI) $\Omega$ which occupies the water and brain tissues.

nodes.name: Standard QSM pipeline
nodes.statement: The standard QSM consists of the following four steps: offset correction, phase unwrapping, background field removal and dipole inversion (see \cref{SchematicProcedure} for the overview of the process). The first three steps extract the local field $b_l$ that is contained in the total field $b$: the offset correction removes/corrects $\theta_0(\boldsymbol{x})$ from $\theta(\boldsymbol{x})$ to obtain $b(\boldsymbol{x})\omega_0B_0TE$ (the offset corrected phase) lying in $(-\pi,\pi]$; the phase unwrapping removes the artificial jumps in the offset corrected phase when estimating the total field $b$; the background field removal eliminates the field induced by the susceptibility outside $\Omega$ such as skulls and nasal cavity.
nodes.origin_citation: Haacke et al. 2015; Schweser et al. 2016; Wang & Liu 2015
nodes.statement_short: QSM pipeline: offset correction, phase unwrapping, background field removal to get local field $b_l$, then dipole inversion.
output: the local field $b_l$ that is contained in the total field $b$

nodes.name: Offset correction
nodes.statement: the offset correction removes/corrects $\theta_0(\boldsymbol{x})$ from $\theta(\boldsymbol{x})$ to obtain $b(\boldsymbol{x})\omega_0B_0TE$ (the offset corrected phase) lying in $(-\pi,\pi]$
nodes.origin_citation: Haacke et al. 2015; Schweser et al. 2016; Wang & Liu 2015
nodes.statement_short: Remove the coil-dependent phase offset $\theta_0$.

nodes.name: Phase unwrapping
nodes.statement: the phase unwrapping removes the artificial jumps in the offset corrected phase when estimating the total field $b$
nodes.origin_citation: Haacke et al. 2015; Schweser et al. 2016; Wang & Liu 2015
nodes.statement_short: Remove artificial $2\pi$ jumps to estimate the total field $b$.

nodes.name: Background field removal
nodes.statement: the background field removal eliminates the field induced by the susceptibility outside $\Omega$ such as skulls and nasal cavity
nodes.origin_citation: Haacke et al. 2015; Schweser et al. 2016; Wang & Liu 2015
nodes.statement_short: Eliminate the field induced by susceptibility outside $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Dipole inversion
nodes.statement_short: Recover $\chi$ in $\Omega$ from the local field $b_l$ given as principal-value convolution with the dipole kernel $d$.

nodes.name: Dipole convolution relation
nodes.statement: b_l(\boldsymbol{x})=\mathrm{pv}\int_{\Omega}d(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})\chi({\boldsymbol y})\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol y},
nodes.label: QSM_Deconv

nodes.name: Dipole kernel in frequency domain $\mathcal D$
nodes.statement:
In the frequency domain, \cref{QSM_Deconv} reads
\begin{align} {\mathscr F}(b_l)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})={\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}){\mathscr F}(\chi)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{\xi_3^2}{|{\boldsymbol{\xi}}|^2}\right){\mathscr F}(\chi)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})
\end{align}
where ${\mathcal D}={\mathscr F}(d)$ is the Fourier transform of $d$ and ${\mathcal D}(\0)=0$  by the definition of $\mathrm{pv}$ \cite{L.deRochefort2010,E.M.Haacke2015}.
nodes.origin_citation: de Rochefort et al. 2010; Haacke et al. 2015
nodes.statement_short: In Fourier space the local field is $\mathcal D(\xi)=1/3-\xi_3^2/|\xi|^2$ times $\mathscr F(\chi)$, with $\mathcal D(0)=0$.

nodes.name: QSM forward model in frequency domain
nodes.statement: {\mathscr F}(b_l)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})={\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}){\mathscr F}(\chi)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{\xi_3^2}{|{\boldsymbol{\xi}}|^2}\right){\mathscr F}(\chi)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})
nodes.origin_citation: de Rochefort et al. 2010; Haacke et al. 2015
nodes.label: QSM_Fou

nodes.name: Ill-posedness of QSM on the critical manifold
nodes.statement: From \eqref{QSM_Fou}, it is easy to see that recovering the susceptibility distribution $\chi$ is ill-posed as ${\mathcal D}=0$ on the critical manifold $\Gamma_0=\left\{{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in{\mathbb R}^3:\xi_1^2+\xi_2^2-2\xi_3^2=0\right\}$.
conclusions: recovering the susceptibility distribution $\chi$ is ill-posed as ${\mathcal D}=0$ on the critical manifold $\Gamma_0=\left\{{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in{\mathbb R}^3:\xi_1^2+\xi_2^2-2\xi_3^2=0\right\}$
nodes.statement_short: Dipole inversion is ill-posed since $\mathcal D$ vanishes on the conic critical manifold $\Gamma_0$.

nodes.name: Truncated K-space division (TKD)
nodes.statement:
One benchmark method, called the truncated K-space division (TKD) \cite{K.Shmueli2009}, finds the approximate solution to \cref{QSM_Fou} via:
\begin{align} \chi_{\hbar}={\mathscr F}^{-1}({\mathcal X}_{\hbar}),~~~\text{where}~~{\mathcal X}_{\hbar}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\frac{\mathrm{sign}({\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}))}{\max\left\{|{\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})|,\hbar\right\}}{\mathscr F}(b_l)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})




\end{align}
with a threshold level $\hbar>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct inversion dividing by $\mathcal D$ truncated at level $\hbar$ in k-space.

nodes.name: TKD solution formula
nodes.statement: \chi_{\hbar}={\mathscr F}^{-1}({\mathcal X}_{\hbar}),~~~\text{where}~~{\mathcal X}_{\hbar}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\frac{\mathrm{sign}({\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}))}{\max\left\{|{\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})|,\hbar\right\}}{\mathscr F}(b_l)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})
nodes.label: TKD

nodes.name: Tikhonov regularization for QSM
nodes.statement:
Another method recovers $\chi$ via solving the following Tikhonov regularization \cite{B.Kressler2010}:
\begin{align} \min_{\chi}~\frac{1}{2}\left\|A\chi-b_l\right\|_2^2+\varepsilon\left\|\chi\right\|_2^2
\end{align}
where $\varepsilon>0$ and $A$ denotes the forward operator that is obtained by discretizing the kernel ${\mathcal D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Least-squares fit of $A\chi$ to $b_l$ with $\ell_2$ penalty $\varepsilon\|\chi\|_2^2$.

nodes.name: Tikhonov regularization model
nodes.statement: \min_{\chi}~\frac{1}{2}\left\|A\chi-b_l\right\|_2^2+\varepsilon\left\|\chi\right\|_2^2
nodes.label: Tikhonov

nodes.name: Regularization based QSM model
nodes.statement:
Mathematically, it is formulated as solving the minimization problem:
\begin{align} \min_{\chi}~F(b_l|\chi)+R(\chi),
\end{align}
where $F(b_l|\chi)$ denotes the data fidelity term and $R(\chi)$ is the regularization term which mostly promotes the sparse approximation of $\chi$ under some linear transformation such as total variation and wavelet frames.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize data fidelity $F(b_l|\chi)$ plus sparsity-promoting regularizer $R(\chi)$.

nodes.name: Generic regularized QSM objective
nodes.statement: \min_{\chi}~F(b_l|\chi)+R(\chi),
nodes.label: Regularization

nodes.name: Integral and differential approaches
nodes.statement: According to the choices of $F(b_l|\chi)$, the regularization based methods can be classified into the \emph{integral approaches} and the \emph{differential approaches} \cite{Y.Kee2017}.

nodes.name: QSM PDE
nodes.statement: -\Delta b_l(\boldsymbol{x})=P(D)\chi(\boldsymbol{x})=\left(-\frac{1}{3}\Delta+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_3^2}\right)\chi(\boldsymbol{x})~~~~~~~\boldsymbol{x}\in\Omega
nodes.origin_citation: Haacke et al. 1999; Seo et al. 2014
nodes.statement_short: $-\Delta b_l=P(D)\chi$ with $P(D)=-\Delta/3+\partial_{x_3}^2$ in $\Omega$.
nodes.label: QSM_PDE

nodes.name: SMV-filtered integral approach
nodes.statement_short: Integral approach with fidelity filtered by spherical mean value filter $S_r$.

nodes.name: SMV integral model
nodes.statement: \min_{\chi}~\frac{1}{2}\left\|S_r\left(A\chi-b_l\right)\right\|_2^2+R(\chi).
nodes.label: IntegralSMV

nodes.name: Harmonic incompatibility
nodes.statement: Whenever the data acquisition is based on the PDE \cref{QSM_PDE}, the measured local field data will be written as the superposition of $b_l$ in \cref{QSM_Deconv} and the ambiguity of $-\Delta$, which will be referred as the \emph{harmonic incompatibility}.
nodes.section: 1.2 Motivations and Contributions of Our Approach
differentia: the measured local field data will be written as the superposition of $b_l$ in \cref{QSM_Deconv} and the ambiguity of $-\Delta$

nodes.name: Magnetostatic Maxwell's equations
nodes.origin_citation: Haacke et al. 1999; Seo et al. 2014
conclusions: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}&=0
\nabla\times\mathbf{B}&=\mu_0\nabla\times{\mathbf M},
nodes.label: MagnetostaticMaxwell

nodes.name: Lorenz sphere correction model
nodes.statement: \mathbf{B}_{\ell}(\boldsymbol{x})=\mathbf{B}(\boldsymbol{x})-\frac{2}{3}\mu_0{\mathbf M}(\boldsymbol{x})
nodes.label: Lorenz

nodes.name: Linear magnetic material approximation
Susceptibility-magnetization approximation
nodes.statement: \chi(\boldsymbol{x})\approx\frac{\mu_0}{B_0}{\mathbf M}(\boldsymbol{x}).
nodes.label: Approx1

nodes.name: Total field $b$
Total field definition
nodes.statement: b(\boldsymbol{x})=\frac{B_{\ell3}(\boldsymbol{x})-B_0}{B_0}
nodes.label: Approx2

nodes.name: Dipole field PDE
assumptions: Combining \cref{MagnetostaticMaxwell,Lorenz,Approx1,Approx2} and taking the third component into account only
conclusions: |{\boldsymbol{\xi}}|^2{\mathscr F}(b)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\left(\frac{1}{3}|{\boldsymbol{\xi}}|^2-\xi_3^2\right){\mathscr F}(\chi)({\boldsymbol{\xi}}),
-\Delta b=P(D)\chi:=\left(-\frac{1}{3}\Delta+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_3^2}\right)\chi.
nodes.statement_short: Maxwell + Lorentz correction give $-\Delta b=P(D)\chi$, defining the operator $P(D)$.

nodes.name: Frequency-domain field relation
nodes.statement: |{\boldsymbol{\xi}}|^2{\mathscr F}(b)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\left(\frac{1}{3}|{\boldsymbol{\xi}}|^2-\xi_3^2\right){\mathscr F}(\chi)({\boldsymbol{\xi}}),
nodes.label: QSM_Fou2

nodes.name: Operator $P(D)$ PDE
nodes.statement: -\Delta b=P(D)\chi:=\left(-\frac{1}{3}\Delta+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_3^2}\right)\chi.
nodes.label: QSM_PDE2

nodes.name: General bounded solution for the total field
nodes.statement:
Then for a given susceptibility distribution $\chi$ (in ${\mathbb R}^3$), the general solution $b$ which is bounded everywhere in ${\mathbb R}^3$ is expressed as
\begin{align} b(\boldsymbol{x})=\int_{{\mathbb R}^3}\Phi(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})\left(-\frac{1}{3}\Delta_{{\boldsymbol y}}+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial y_3^2}\right)\chi({\boldsymbol y})\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol y}+b_0
\end{align}
where $b_0$ is some constant, and $\Phi(\boldsymbol{x})=1/\left(4\pi|\boldsymbol{x}|\right)$.
assumptions: for a given susceptibility distribution $\chi$ (in ${\mathbb R}^3$)
conclusions: b(\boldsymbol{x})=\int_{{\mathbb R}^3}\Phi(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})\left(-\frac{1}{3}\Delta_{{\boldsymbol y}}+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial y_3^2}\right)\chi({\boldsymbol y})\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol y}+b_0
nodes.statement_short: Bounded solutions of $-\Delta b=P(D)\chi$ are Newton-potential convolutions plus a constant $b_0$.

nodes.name: General solution
nodes.statement: b(\boldsymbol{x})=\int_{{\mathbb R}^3}\Phi(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})\left(-\frac{1}{3}\Delta_{{\boldsymbol y}}+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial y_3^2}\right)\chi({\boldsymbol y})\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol y}+b_0
nodes.label: GeneralSolution

nodes.name: Zero phase offset ($b_0=0$) forward model
Total field forward model
nodes.statement: b(\boldsymbol{x})=\int_{{\mathbb R}^3}\Phi(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})\left(-\frac{1}{3}\Delta_{{\boldsymbol y}}+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial y_3^2}\right)\chi({\boldsymbol y})\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol y}
nodes.label: Forward1

nodes.name: Equivalence with principal value representation
nodes.statement:
Since \cite[Proposition A.1.]{J.K.Choi2014} has discussed the equivalence between \cref{Forward1} and the following representation in the literature
\begin{align} b(\boldsymbol{x})=\mathrm{pv}\int_{{\mathbb R}^3}d(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})\chi({\boldsymbol y})\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol y},
\end{align}
we shall use \cref{Forward1} in the rest of this paper. Note that \cref{Forward1} avoids the singularity of the kernel $d(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})$ in \cref{Forward_Convention} as $\Phi(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})$ is locally integrable near $\boldsymbol{x}={\boldsymbol y}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Choi et al. the Newton-potential model is equivalent to the pv dipole convolution and avoids the kernel singularity.
nodes.label: RK211

nodes.name: Principal value forward model
nodes.statement: b(\boldsymbol{x})=\mathrm{pv}\int_{{\mathbb R}^3}d(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})\chi({\boldsymbol y})\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol y},
nodes.label: Forward_Convention

nodes.name: Poisson background field removal (LBV)
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
nodes.statement_short: Get local field $b_l$ by solving Poisson's equation $-\Delta b_l=-\Delta b$ in $\Omega$ with zero Dirichlet data.

nodes.name: Laplacian boundary value problem
nodes.statement:
\left\{\begin{array}{rcll}
-\Delta b_l\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&-\Delta b&\text{in}~\Omega \vspace{0.125em}\\
b_l\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&0&\text{on}~\partial\Omega.
\end{array}\right.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
nodes.label: LBV

nodes.name: Characterization of harmonic incompatibility
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega\subseteq{\mathbb R}^3$ be an open and bounded set with $C^1$ boundary $\partial\Omega$. Let $b$ satisfy \cref{Forward1} for a given $\chi$ compactly supported in ${\mathbb R}^3$, and let $b_l:\overline{\Omega}\to{\mathbb R}$ be obtained from \cref{LBV}. If we extend $b_l$ into ${\mathbb R}^3$ by assigning $b_l(\boldsymbol{x})=0$ for $\boldsymbol{x}\notin\Omega$, then we have the followings:
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
assumptions: $\Omega\subseteq{\mathbb R}^3$ be an open and bounded set with $C^1$ boundary $\partial\Omega$
$b$ satisfy \cref{Forward1} for a given $\chi$ compactly supported in ${\mathbb R}^3$
we extend $b_l$ into ${\mathbb R}^3$ by assigning $b_l(\boldsymbol{x})=0$ for $\boldsymbol{x}\notin\Omega$
conclusions: we have the followings:
nodes.statement_short: Measured local field from LBV = true local field plus incompatibility $v$, harmonic off $\partial\Omega$ with Laplacian a surface measure on $\partial\Omega$.
nodes.label: Th1

nodes.name: Theorem 2.1 part 1: incompatibility decomposition
nodes.statement:
There exists $v(x)$ such that
\begin{align} b_l(\boldsymbol{x})=\int_{\Omega}\Phi(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})\left(-\frac{1}{3}\Delta_{{\boldsymbol y}}+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial y_3^2}\right)\chi({\boldsymbol y})\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol y}+v(\boldsymbol{x})
\end{align}
for $\boldsymbol{x}\in{\mathbb R}^3$, and $v(\boldsymbol{x})$ satisfies
\begin{align} \int_{{\mathbb R}^3}v(\boldsymbol{x})\left(-\Delta\varphi\right)(\boldsymbol{x})\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{x}=\int_{\partial\Omega}\left[\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{n}}(\boldsymbol{x})-\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm e}}{\partial\boldsymbol{n}}(\boldsymbol{x})\right]\varphi(\boldsymbol{x})\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\boldsymbol{x})
\end{align}
for $\varphi\in C_0^{\infty}({\mathbb R}^3)$, where $v_{\mathrm i}$ and $v_{\mathrm e}$ denote the restriction of $v$ in $\overline{\Omega}$ and ${\mathbb R}^3\setminus\Omega$ respectively, and $\boldsymbol{n}$ denotes the outward unit normal vector of $\partial\Omega$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
assumptions: $v_{\mathrm i}$ and $v_{\mathrm e}$ denote the restriction of $v$ in $\overline{\Omega}$ and ${\mathbb R}^3\setminus\Omega$ respectively, and $\boldsymbol{n}$ denotes the outward unit normal vector of $\partial\Omega$
conclusions: There exists $v(x)$ such that
nodes.statement_short: $b_l$ equals the $\Omega$-restricted potential of $P(D)\chi$ plus $v$, whose distributional Laplacian is the normal-derivative jump on $\partial\Omega$.

nodes.name: New forward modeling with incompatibility
nodes.statement: b_l(\boldsymbol{x})=\int_{\Omega}\Phi(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})\left(-\frac{1}{3}\Delta_{{\boldsymbol y}}+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial y_3^2}\right)\chi({\boldsymbol y})\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol y}+v(\boldsymbol{x})
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
nodes.label: NewModeling

nodes.name: Distributional Laplacian of incompatibility
nodes.statement: \int_{{\mathbb R}^3}v(\boldsymbol{x})\left(-\Delta\varphi\right)(\boldsymbol{x})\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{x}=\int_{\partial\Omega}\left[\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{n}}(\boldsymbol{x})-\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm e}}{\partial\boldsymbol{n}}(\boldsymbol{x})\right]\varphi(\boldsymbol{x})\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\boldsymbol{x})
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
nodes.label: DistLapIncompatibility

nodes.name: Theorem 2.1 part 2: non-vanishing surface measure
nodes.statement:
Moreover, we have
\begin{align} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{n}}-\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm e}}{\partial\boldsymbol{n}}\neq0~~~~\text{almost everywhere on}~\partial\Omega
\end{align}
whenever $P(D)\chi\neq0$ in $\Omega$. Hence, $-\Delta v=0$ in ${\mathbb R}^3\setminus\partial\Omega$, and $-\Delta v\neq0$ on $\partial\Omega$ in this case.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
conclusions: Hence, $-\Delta v=0$ in ${\mathbb R}^3\setminus\partial\Omega$, and $-\Delta v\neq0$ on $\partial\Omega$ in this case.
nodes.statement_short: If $P(D)\chi\neq0$ in $\Omega$, the normal-derivative jump of $v$ is a.e. nonzero, so $-\Delta v$ is a nonvanishing surface measure on $\partial\Omega$.

nodes.name: Nonvanishing normal derivative jump
nodes.statement: \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm i}}{\partial\boldsymbol{n}}-\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm e}}{\partial\boldsymbol{n}}\neq0~~~~\text{almost everywhere on}~\partial\Omega
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
nodes.label: NonVanishingSurfMeas

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
nodes.statement_short: Represent $b_l$ via the Dirichlet Green's function, split off a harmonic corrector to define $v$, and apply Green's identity on both sides of $\partial\Omega$. Part 2 by contradiction using analyticity (unique continuation) of harmonic functions.

nodes.name: Rewrite LBV via $-\Delta b=P(D)\chi$
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite LBV via $-\Delta b=P(D)\chi$

nodes.name: Unique continuation by analyticity
nodes.statement: Then since $-\Delta v=0$ in $B(\boldsymbol{x},r)$ and $v=v_{\mathrm e}=-\widetilde{b}_l$ in $B(\boldsymbol{x},r)\cap\left({\mathbb R}^3\setminus\overline{\Omega}\right)$, it follows that $v=-\widetilde{b}_l$ in $B(\boldsymbol{x},r)$ by the analyticity of $v$ in $B(\boldsymbol{x},r)$. Since this means that $v=v_{\mathrm i}=-\widetilde{b}_l$ in $B(\boldsymbol{x},r)\cap\Omega$, together with the fact that $v_{\mathrm i}$ is harmonic in $\Omega$, we have $v_{\mathrm i}=-\widetilde{b}_l$ in $\Omega$ by the analyticity of $v_{\mathrm i}$ in $\Omega$. Since $v=-\widetilde{b}_l$ on $\partial\Omega$, we have $v=-\widetilde{b}_l$ in ${\mathbb R}^3$.

nodes.name: Origin of the incompatibility
nodes.statement: From the proof of \cref{Th1},  the incompatibility $v$ in \cref{NewModeling} is from the boundary condition of \cref{LBV} which is not related to the regularity of $\chi$. More precisely, $v_{\mathrm i}$ inside $\Omega$ is generated by the information of the unknown true local field $\widetilde{b}_l$ on $\partial\Omega$ so that the boundary condition of \cref{LBV} is matched. In addition, it is obvious that $v_{\mathrm e}$ outside $\Omega$ is due to the information loss outside $\Omega$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
nodes.statement_short: The incompatibility stems from LBV's boundary condition: $v_i$ from the true local field on $\partial\Omega$, $v_e$ from information loss outside $\Omega$.
nodes.label: RK221

nodes.name: Nonvanishing surface measure in QSM
nodes.statement: Notice that $P(D)$ is a ``wave type'' differential operator (by considering $x_3$ as the time variable). Indeed, the proof of \cref{NonVanishingSurfMeas} tells us that if $P(D)\chi=0$ in $\Omega$, such $\chi$ has a wave type structure in $\Omega$ regardless of its regularity, whereas the susceptibility of human brain does not have such a wave type structure \cite{J.K.Choi2014}. Hence in QSM, it follows that $-\Delta v$ defined as \cref{DistLapIncompatibility} is a nonvanishing surface measure on $\partial\Omega$, i.e. $-\Delta v=0$ in ${\mathbb R}^3\setminus\partial\Omega$, but $-\Delta v\neq0$ on $\partial\Omega$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
nodes.statement_short: Since brain susceptibility lacks wave-type structure, $-\Delta v$ is a nonvanishing surface measure on $\partial\Omega$ in QSM.
nodes.label: RK222

nodes.name: Grid index set $\mathbb O$ and discrete ROI
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathbb O}=\left\{0,\cdots,N_1-1\right\}\times\left\{0,\cdots,N_2-1\right\}\times\left\{0,\cdots,N_3-1\right\}$ denote the set of indices of $N_1\times N_2\times N_3$ grids, and let $\Omega\subseteq{\mathbb O}$ denote the set of indices corresponding to the ROI.

nodes.name: Discrete boundary $\partial\Omega$
nodes.statement: Denote $\partial\Omega$ to be the indices of the boundary of ROI $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Image space $\mathcal I_3$
nodes.statement: Finally, the space of real valued functions defined on ${\mathbb O}$ is denoted as ${\mathcal I}_3\simeq{\mathbb R}^{N_1\times N_2\times N_3}$.

nodes.name: Discrete forward model with incompatibility
nodes.statement_short: Measured local field modeled as $b_l=A\chi+v+\eta$: dipole forward operator, harmonic incompatibility, and noise.

nodes.name: Discrete harmonic incompatibility
nodes.statement:
We observe that in the discrete setting, \cref{DistLapIncompatibility} in \cref{Th1} can be understood as
\begin{align} {\mathscr L} v=0\quad\text{in}\quad{\mathbb O}\setminus\partial\Omega\quad\text{ and }\quad {\mathscr L} v\neq0\quad\text{on}\quad\partial\Omega
\end{align}
with the discrete Laplacian ${\mathscr L}$, as ${\mathscr L} v$ is supported on $\partial\Omega$.
conclusions: {\mathscr L} v=0\quad\text{in}\quad{\mathbb O}\setminus\partial\Omega\quad\text{ and }\quad {\mathscr L} v\neq0\quad\text{on}\quad\partial\Omega
nodes.statement_short: Discretely, $\mathscr L v$ vanishes off $\partial\Omega$ and is nonzero on it.

nodes.name: Discrete harmonic incompatibility
nodes.statement: {\mathscr L} v=0\quad\text{in}\quad{\mathbb O}\setminus\partial\Omega\quad\text{ and }\quad {\mathscr L} v\neq0\quad\text{on}\quad\partial\Omega
nodes.label: DiscreteHarmonicIncompatibility

nodes.name: HIRE model (wavelet frame)
nodes.statement_short: Jointly fit $A\chi+v$ to $b_l$ with $\ell_1$ penalty on $\mathscr L v$ and isotropic wavelet-frame sparsity on $\chi$.

nodes.name: Frame-HIRE objective
nodes.statement: \min_{\chi,v\in{\mathcal I}_3}~\frac{1}{2}\left\|A\chi+v-b_l\right\|_{\Sigma}^2+\lambda\left\|{\mathscr L} v\right\|_1+\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}
nodes.label: WaveletFrameHIRE

nodes.name: Isotropic $\ell_1$ norm of wavelet frame coefficients
Isotropic wavelet frame norm
nodes.statement: \left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}:=\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb O}}\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\gamma_l[{\boldsymbol k}]\left(\sum_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in{\mathbb B}}\left|\left(W_{l,\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\chi\right)[{\boldsymbol k}]\right|^2\right)^{1/2}.
nodes.label: IsoTropicWaveletFrame

nodes.name: HIRE reduces to integral and differential approaches
nodes.statement_short: With $v\equiv0$ HIRE is the integral approach; with $v=b_l-A\chi$ it is an $\ell_1$-fidelity differential approach.
nodes.label: RK231

nodes.name: Heuristic effect of harmonic incompatibility on low frequencies
nodes.statement: Even though more rigorous theoretical analysis is needed, we can somehow explain the effect of harmonic incompatibility in this manner; since the standard arguments on the harmonic functions (e.g. \cite{Evans2010}) tell us that $v$ is smooth and satisfies the mean value property except on $\partial\Omega$, it has slow variations on this region. As a consequence, it mostly affects the low frequency components in $b_l$ compared to the noise which mainly affects the high frequency components. Together with the fact that the critical manifold $\Gamma_0$ forms a conic manifold in the frequency domain, the harmonic incompatibility $v$ in $b_l$ mainly leads to the loss of ${\mathscr F}(\chi)$ in low frequency components.
nodes.statement_short: Being smooth off $\partial\Omega$, $v$ mainly corrupts low frequencies of $b_l$, causing loss of low-frequency $\mathscr F(\chi)$ near $\Gamma_0$.

nodes.name: Nonlinear fidelity HIRE variant
nodes.statement: We would like to mention that the formulation of HIRE model is not limited to \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE}. In fact, we can use the nonlinear fidelity term $F(b_l|\chi,v)=\frac{1}{2}\left\|e^{i(A\chi+v)\omega_0B_0TE}-e^{ib_l\omega_0B_0TE}\right\|_{\Sigma}^2$ to further compensate the errors in phase unwrapping, which will be more coincident with the GRE signal model \cite{Y.Kee2017,T.Liu2013}.
nodes.statement_short: HIRE can use a nonlinear complex-exponential fidelity to compensate phase unwrapping errors.

nodes.name: Split reformulation of HIRE
nodes.statement_short: Constrained reformulation of HIRE with auxiliary variables $d=W\chi$, $e=\mathscr L v$, $f=A\chi$, $g=v$.

nodes.name: Split Bregman algorithm for HIRE
nodes.statement_short: ADMM/split Bregman: alternately update $(\chi,v)$ by least squares, $(d,e,f,g)$ by thresholding/weighted averaging, then Bregman variables.
nodes.label: Algorithm1

nodes.name: Main iteration loop
One split Bregman iteration
nodes.statement_short: Update primal variables, auxiliary variables, then Bregman variables.

nodes.name: Update $\chi$ and $v$
Update $d$, $e$, $f$, $g$
Update Bregman variables
$\chi$ and $v$ subproblems
nodes.statement:
\chi^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{\chi}~\frac{\beta}{2}\|A\chi-f^k+r^k\|_2^2+\frac{\beta}{2}\|W\chi-d^k+p^k\|_2^2 \\
v^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{v}~\frac{\beta}{2}\|v-g^k+s^k\|_2^2+\frac{\beta}{2}\|{\mathscr L} v-e^k+q^k\|_2^2
nodes.label: chisubproblem

nodes.name: $d,e,f,g$ subproblems
nodes.statement:
d^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_d~\left\|\gamma\cdot d\right\|_{1,2}+\frac{\beta}{2}\|d-W\chi^{k+1}-p^k\|_2^2 \\
e^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_e~\lambda\left\|e\right\|_1+\frac{\beta}{2}\|e-{\mathscr L} v^{k+1}-q^k\|_2^2 \\
f^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_f~\frac{1}{2}\|f+g^k-b_l\|_{\Sigma}^2+\frac{\beta}{2}\|f-A\chi^{k+1}-r^k\|_2^2 \\
g^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_g~\frac{1}{2}\|g+f^{k+1}-b_l\|_{\Sigma}^2+\frac{\beta}{2}\|g-v^{k+1}-s^k\|_2^2
nodes.label: dsubproblem

nodes.name: Closed form subproblem solutions
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that each subproblem has a closed form solution.
conclusions: each subproblem has a closed form solution

nodes.name: Explicit $\chi$ and $v$ updates
nodes.statement:
\chi^{k+1}&=\big(A^TA+I\big)^{-1}\big[A^T(f^k-r^k)+W^T(d^k-p^k)\big] \\
v^{k+1}&=\big(I+{\mathscr L}^T{\mathscr L}\big)^{-1}\big[g^k-s^k+{\mathscr L}^T(e^k-q^k)\big].
nodes.label: chisubexplicit

nodes.name: Soft-thresholding updates for $d$ and $e$
nodes.statement:
d^{k+1}&={\mathcal T}_{\gamma/\beta}\big(W\chi^{k+1}+p^k\big) \\
e^{k+1}&=\max\big(|{\mathscr L} v^{k+1}+q^k|-\lambda/\beta,0\big)\mathrm{sign}\big({\mathscr L} v^{k+1}+q^k\big).
nodes.label: dsubexplicit

nodes.name: Isotropic soft thresholding $\mathcal T_\gamma$
nodes.statement_short: Shrink each level's coefficient vector across bands by its joint magnitude minus $\gamma_l$, leaving the low-pass band untouched.

nodes.name: Explicit $f$ and $g$ updates
nodes.statement:
f^{k+1}&=\big(\Sigma+\beta I\big)^{-1}\big[\Sigma(b_l-g^k)+\beta(A\chi^{k+1}+r^k)\big] \\
g^{k+1}&=\big(\Sigma+\beta I\big)^{-1}\big[\Sigma(b_l-f^{k+1})+\beta(v^{k+1}+s^k)\big]
nodes.label: fsubexplicit

nodes.name: Convergence of split Bregman for HIRE
nodes.statement: Note that, since our model \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE} is convex, it can be verified that \cref{Algorithm1} converges to the minimizer of \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE} by following the framework of \cite[Theorem 3.2.]{J.F.Cai2009/10}, whenever it has the unique global minimizer.
assumptions: whenever it has the unique global minimizer
conclusions: \cref{Algorithm1} converges to the minimizer of \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE}
nodes.statement_short: The split Bregman iteration converges to the unique minimizer of the convex HIRE model.

nodes.statement: \min_{\chi\in{\mathcal I}_3}~\frac{1}{2}\left\|A\chi-b_l\right\|_{\Sigma}^2+\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}

nodes.name: HIRE outperforms existing approaches on brain phantom
nodes.statement: We can see that both the Frame-HIRE and the TGV-HIRE consistently outperform the existing direct approaches, the integral approaches, and the differential approaches in both cases.
conclusions: both the Frame-HIRE and the TGV-HIRE consistently outperform the existing direct approaches, the integral approaches, and the differential approaches in both cases

nodes.name: TGV-HIRE is about 3 times slower than Frame-HIRE
nodes.statement: As a consequence, the CPU time of the TGV-HIRE becomes approximately $3$ times longer than approximately $11.5\mathrm{min}$ of the Frame-HIRE as shown in \cref{ComparisonTimePhantom}, which shows that the TGV regularization approach may not be suitable for the real clinical applications.
conclusions: the CPU time of the TGV-HIRE becomes approximately $3$ times longer than approximately $11.5\mathrm{min}$ of the Frame-HIRE

nodes.name: HIRE reduces boundary-propagated streaking artifacts in vivo
nodes.statement: It is also worth noting that the HIRE models can reduce the streaking artifacts which propagate from $\partial\Omega$ into $\Omega$ as well as the shadow artifacts.
nodes.section: 3.2 Experiments on In Vivo MR Data
conclusions: the HIRE models can reduce the streaking artifacts which propagate from $\partial\Omega$ into $\Omega$ as well as the shadow artifacts

nodes.name: Quasi-affine system
nodes.genus: the collection of the dilations and the shifts of the elements in ${\boldsymbol \Psi}$

nodes.name: Quasi-affine system
nodes.statement: {\mathscr X}({\boldsymbol \Psi})=\left\{\psi_{\alpha,n,{\boldsymbol k}}:1\leq\alpha\leq r,~n\in{\mathbb Z},~{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d\right\},
nodes.label: QASystem

nodes.name: Quasi-affine framelet dilations
nodes.statement:
\psi_{\alpha,n,{\boldsymbol k}}=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}
2^{\frac{nd}{2}}\psi_{\alpha}(2^n\cdot-{\boldsymbol k})~~&~~n\geq 0;\vspace{0.125em}\\
2^{nd}\psi_{\alpha}(2^n\cdot-2^{n}{\boldsymbol k})~~&~~n<0.
\end{array}\right.
nodes.label: QAFramelet

nodes.name: Tight wavelet frame
nodes.statement:
We say that ${\mathscr X}({\boldsymbol \Psi})$ is a tight wavelet frame on $L_2({\mathbb R}^d)$ if we have
\begin{align} \left\|f\right\|_{L_2({\mathbb R}^d)}^2=\sum_{\alpha=1}^r\sum_{n\in{\mathbb Z}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d}\left|\left\langle f,\psi_{\alpha,n,{\boldsymbol k}}\right\rangle\right|^2
\end{align}
for every $f\in L_2({\mathbb R}^d)$.

nodes.name: Tight frame identity
nodes.statement: \left\|f\right\|_{L_2({\mathbb R}^d)}^2=\sum_{\alpha=1}^r\sum_{n\in{\mathbb Z}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d}\left|\left\langle f,\psi_{\alpha,n,{\boldsymbol k}}\right\rangle\right|^2
nodes.label: TightFrame

nodes.name: Framelet and canonical coefficient
nodes.statement: In this case, each $\psi_{\alpha}$ is called a (tight) framelet, and $\left\langle f,\psi_{\alpha,n,{\boldsymbol k}}\right\rangle$ is called the canonical coefficient of $f$.

nodes.name: Refinable function and refinement mask
nodes.definiendum: refinable function $\phi$ with a refinement mask $q_0$

nodes.name: Refinement equation
nodes.statement: \phi=2^d\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d}q_0[{\boldsymbol k}]\phi(2\cdot-{\boldsymbol k}).
nodes.label: MRA-RF

nodes.name: MRA based framelet construction
Framelet masks relation
nodes.statement: \psi_{\alpha}=2^d\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d}q_{\alpha}[{\boldsymbol k}]\phi(2\cdot-{\boldsymbol k}),~~~~~\alpha=1,\cdots,r.
nodes.label: MRA-Fra

nodes.name: High pass and low pass filters
nodes.statement: The sequences $q_1,\cdots,q_r$ are called wavelet frame mask or the high pass filters of the system, and the refinement mask $q_0$ is also called the low pass filter.
nodes.definiendum: wavelet frame mask or the high pass filters

nodes.name: Unitary extension principle (UEP)
nodes.statement:
Briefly speaking, as long as $\left\{q_0,q_1,\cdots,q_r\right\}$ are compactly supported and their Fourier series $\widehat{q}_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d}q_{\alpha}[{\boldsymbol k}]e^{-i{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\cdot{\boldsymbol k}}$ satisfy
\begin{align} \sum_{\alpha=0}^r\left|\widehat{q}_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})\right|^2=1~~~~\text{and}~~~~\sum_{\alpha=0}^r\widehat{q}_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})\overline{\widehat{q}_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}+\boldsymbol{\nu})}=0
\end{align}
for all $\boldsymbol{\nu}\in\left\{0,\pi\right\}^d\setminus\left\{\0\right\}$ and ${\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in[-\pi,\pi]^d$, the quasi-affine system ${\mathscr X}({\boldsymbol \Psi})$ with ${\boldsymbol \Psi}=\left\{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_r\right\}$ defined by \cref{MRA-Fra} forms a tight frame of $L_2({\mathbb R}^d)$, and the filters $\left\{q_0,q_1,\cdots,q_r\right\}$ form a discrete tight frame on $\ell_2({\mathbb Z}^d)$ \cite{B.Dong2013}.
conclusions: the quasi-affine system ${\mathscr X}({\boldsymbol \Psi})$ with ${\boldsymbol \Psi}=\left\{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_r\right\}$ defined by \cref{MRA-Fra} forms a tight frame of $L_2({\mathbb R}^d)$
the filters $\left\{q_0,q_1,\cdots,q_r\right\}$ form a discrete tight frame on $\ell_2({\mathbb Z}^d)$
nodes.statement_short: If the mask Fourier series satisfy the UEP identities, the MRA framelets form a tight frame of $L_2(\mathbb R^d)$.

nodes.name: UEP conditions
nodes.statement: \sum_{\alpha=0}^r\left|\widehat{q}_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})\right|^2=1~~~~\text{and}~~~~\sum_{\alpha=0}^r\widehat{q}_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})\overline{\widehat{q}_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}+\boldsymbol{\nu})}=0
nodes.label: UEP

nodes.name: Haar framelet
nodes.statement_short: Piecewise constant B-spline: box refinable function, Haar framelet, filters $\frac12[1,1]$ and $\frac12[1,-1]$ satisfy UEP.
nodes.label: ExA1

nodes.name: Tensor product multivariate masks
Tensor product framelets
Tensor product framelets form a tight frame
nodes.statement: If the univariate masks $\left\{q_{\alpha}\right\}$ are constructed from UEP, then we can verify that $\left\{q_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\}$ satisfies \cref{UEP} and thus ${\mathscr X}({\boldsymbol \Psi})$ with ${\boldsymbol \Psi}=\left\{\psi_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}:\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\{0,\cdots,r\}^d\setminus\{\0\}\right\}$ forms a tight frame for $L_2({\mathbb R}^d)$.
assumptions: the univariate masks $\left\{q_{\alpha}\right\}$ are constructed from UEP
conclusions: $\left\{q_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\}$ satisfies \cref{UEP}

${\mathscr X}({\boldsymbol \Psi})$ with ${\boldsymbol \Psi}=\left\{\psi_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}:\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\{0,\cdots,r\}^d\setminus\{\0\}\right\}$ forms a tight frame for $L_2({\mathbb R}^d)$

nodes.name: Discrete image space $\mathcal I_d$
nodes.statement: In the discrete setting, let ${\mathcal I}_d\simeq{\mathbb R}^{N_1\times\cdots\times N_d}$ be the space of real valued functions defined on a regular grid $\left\{0,1,\cdots,N_1-1\right\}\times\cdots\times\left\{0,1,\cdots,N_d-1\right\}$.

nodes.name: Fast framelet decomposition (analysis operator) $W$
nodes.definiendum: fast framelet decomposition, or the analysis operator

nodes.name: Framelet decomposition
nodes.statement: Wu=\left\{W_{l,\boldsymbol{\alpha}}u:(l,\boldsymbol{\alpha})\in\left(\left\{0,\cdots,L-1\right\}\times{\mathbb B}\right)\cup\left\{(L-1,\0)\right\}\right\}

nodes.name: Frame coefficients $W_{l,\alpha}u$
nodes.statement_short: Level-$l$ band-$\alpha$ coefficients are discrete convolutions with upsampled cascaded filters $q_{l,\alpha}$.

nodes.name: Cascaded filters
nodes.statement:
q_{l,\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\widetilde{q}_{l,\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\circledast\widetilde{q}_{l-1,\0}\circledast\cdots\circledast\widetilde{q}_{0,\0}~~\text{with}~~\widetilde{q}_{l,\boldsymbol{\alpha}}[{\boldsymbol k}]=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}
q_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}[2^{-l}{\boldsymbol k}],&{\boldsymbol k}\in 2^l{\mathbb Z}^d\vspace{0.125em}\\
0,&{\boldsymbol k}\notin 2^l{\mathbb Z}^d.
\end{array}\right.

nodes.name: Synthesis operator $W^T$
nodes.statement: We denote by $W^T$, the adjoint of $W$, the fast reconstruction (or the synthesis operator).

nodes.name: Perfect reconstruction $W^TW=I$
nodes.statement: Then by UEP \cref{UEP}, we have $W^TW=I$.
conclusions: $W^TW=I$
